study.title: Ruth 1 - Grief, return and providence at the beginning of the harvest
study.overview: The chapter opens with a crisis in Bethlehem of Judah: famine, migration to Moab, and the death of Elimelech and his two sons leave Naomi without husband and without heirs. When she hears that the LORD has returned to give bread to his people, she decides to return to Judah. On the way, there is the contrast between Orphah, who goes back, and Ruth, who clings to Naomi with surprising fidelity and confesses that the people and God of Naomi will also be theirs. As they come to Bethlehem, the city is moved, and Naomi interprets its own history as bitterness under the hand of the Almighty. The chapter ends with a discrete sign of hope: they arrive at the beginning of the harvest of barley.

outline.title: Hunger, change and losses in Moabe
outline.explanation: The narrative begins in the time of the judges, marked by instability. The famine leads a family from Bethlehem to Moab, but there the man dies, then the two sons also, and Naomi is forsaken with the daughter-in-one.

outline.title: The return and decision of Ruth
outline.explanation: Hearing that the LORD visited his people with bread, Naomi returns to Judah. She exhorts the nores to return to their homes; Orphah accepts the farewell, but Ruth insists on accompanying her, making a declaration of allegiance to the people, to the land, and to the God of Israel.

outline.title: Arrival to Bethlehem and sign of hope
outline.explanation: The return of Noemi and Ruth causes commotion in Bethlehem. Naomy asks to be called Mara, because he sees his life marked by bitterness. Still, the chapter closes with a providential detail: the arrival occurs at the beginning of the barley harvest.

study.context: The chapter itself places the events on the days when they judged the judges, that is, in a period of national disorder in Israel. The notes provided mention that the famine probably hit the mountainous region of Judah and that Bethlehem was a small town in that area. They also indicate Moab as the land to the southeast of Judah, where there could be enough rain when it was lacking in Judah. The notes associate the beginning of the harvest of barley at the end of March or early April, and observe that the arrival in Bethlehem occurs at an opportune time for survival and provision.
study.theology: The chapter teaches God's sovereignty amidst pain without hiding human suffering. Naomi interprets his story as distress from the hand of the LORD, and the text does not immediately correct this reading; he keeps it in tension with a greater frame of providence. At the same time, the chapter shows God acting in an ordinary way: the news of bread in Bethlehem, the decision to return, the unexpected fidelity of Ruth and the arrival at the beginning of the harvest are pieces of a silent divine conduct. Ruth's confession is theologically central: she abandons her old religious and social connection to join the people of the LORD and the God of Israel himself. Thus, the chapter combines mourning, alliance and hope, preparing the restoration that will come.

scholarViews.insight: The notes highlight that God "gives good things" and acts for providence behind the common events; the mention of the sustenance in Bethlehem frames the narrative among similar divine acts.

The observation that Naomy and Ruth arrives at the beginning of the harvest of barley highlights the providential opportunity of the moment: they arrive when there is already provision and possibility of sustenance.
The note identifies the beginning of the barley harvest as the beginning of spring, shortly after Easter, which helps to understand why their arrival in Bethlehem is especially significant.

questions: What does Naoi's reaction teach about bringing God his own bitterness without makeup the pain?
How is Ruth's decision more than family loyalty and becomes a confession of faith?
How does the detail of the "prince of the barley harvest" help to read God's providence in difficult times?
study.practice: Read your losses without pretending before God, but don't interpret pain as the final word. The chapter encourages itself to turn to the place of promise when there is "pão" again, to welcome people who choose the path of faith with concrete loyalty and to realize that God often guides through simple signs and daily life. In practice, this can mean: persevering in communion with God's people, sustaining bonds of fidelity in times of crisis and maintaining hope even when life seems empty, because the Lord may be preparing provision at the right time.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not allow to safely determine under which judge occurred the facts; there are only varied hypotheses. It is also not possible to affirm, based only on the notes, the exact date of the narrative or external historical details beyond what was explicitly indicated. Noemi's reading of the hand of the Lord is preserved as an interpretation of the character, not as a total and exhaustive explanation of the text.
